definition: In artificial neural networks, a convolutional layer is a type of network layer that applies a convolution operation to the input.
details: Convolutional layers are some of the primary building blocks of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a class of neural network most commonly applied to images, video, audio, and other data that have the property of uniform translational symmetry. The convolution operation in a convolutional layer involves sliding a small window (called a kernel or filter) across the input data and computing the dot product between the values in the kernel and the input at each position. This process creates a feature map that represents detected features in the input.

explainer.lead: A convolutional layer scans its input with a small filter and turns the results into a map of detected features. It is a core building block of convolutional neural networks, which are widely used for images, video, and audio.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sliding a small stencil across a picture to look for the same kind of clue everywhere. At each stop, you combine the stencil with the part underneath and write down a score. All those scores form a new map showing where the clues appear.
tiers.practitioner: Use convolutional layers as CNN building blocks for image, video, audio, or other inputs with uniform translational symmetry. Set up a kernel, slide it across the input, and compute a dot product at every position to produce a feature map. Keep the distinction between the kernel, the layer, and the resulting feature map clear when configuring or debugging a network.
tiers.paperLevel: At one window position, the output is y = sum_i(k_i * x_i), where k_i are kernel values and x_i are the corresponding input values. Evaluating this dot product as the kernel slides across the input produces a feature map representing detected features. Convolutional layers are most commonly applied to data with uniform translational symmetry, including images, video, and audio.

explainer.example: For an input window [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and kernel [[1, 0], [0, -1]], the dot product is 1*1 + 2*0 + 3*0 + 4*(-1) = -3. The value -3 becomes one entry in the feature map; sliding the kernel and repeating fills in the other entries.

usedIn.name: Image processing
usedIn.detail: Convolutional layers build feature maps that represent features detected across an image.

usedIn.name: Video analysis
usedIn.detail: CNNs use convolutional layers to apply the same filtering operation across video input.

usedIn.name: Audio processing
usedIn.detail: Convolutional layers scan audio input with kernels and produce maps of detected features.

explainer.intuition: Instead of treating every position differently, a convolutional layer moves the same small filter across the input. Each position receives a score based on how the kernel combines with the values underneath it, and together those scores describe detected features.
howItWorks: Start with the input data and a small window of values called a kernel or filter.
Place the kernel over one position of the input.
Compute the dot product of the kernel values and the input values in that window.
Slide the kernel to the next position and repeat the calculation.
Collect the results into a feature map representing detected features.
explainer.whyItMatters: Convolutional layers are primary building blocks of CNNs. Their sliding-filter operation provides a direct way to detect features across data with uniform translational symmetry, including images, video, and audio.
misconceptions: The kernel is not the whole layer; it is the small filter that the layer slides across the input.
The output is not just one number for the whole input; the position-by-position results form a feature map.
A convolutional layer is a network component, not an entire convolutional neural network.
